concepts.title: Distance
concepts.claim: Distance adds all path lengths and is non-negative.

concepts.title: Displacement
concepts.claim: In one dimension, displacement is final minus initial position in a declared positive direction.

concepts.title: Signed v-t Area (Displacement)
concepts.claim: Signed area between velocity–time graph and time axis gives displacement over the interval.

concepts.title: v-t Area Magnitudes (Distance)
concepts.claim: Distance is the sum of positive area magnitudes, splitting at every sign change.

lessons.title: First, find your position on the line
lessons.intro: Imagine a straight corridor. We choose a door as 0 m and right as positive.
lessons.caption: The numbers are positions measured from the door. They are not distances already walked.

blocks.text: It says where you are: 4 m to the right of the door. A position of −2 m means 2 m to its left.
The symbol x means position. The sign tells us which side of our chosen zero we mean.
Trace from 0 to +4. Then trace back to 0. The second move goes left, even though every point along it is at 0 m or above.

lessons.takeaway: Say it aloud: position tells me where I am. The direction of my movement tells me which way I am going.

lessons.title: Your turn · Do one small step at a time
lessons.intro: Use the empty number line. Mark your answers before checking them.
lessons.caption: Use different marks for a position and a movement arrow.

blocks.text: Mark −2 m. Is this left or right of the origin?
Start at +1 m. Draw an arrow 3 m left. Label where it ends.
A different move starts at −2 m and finishes at +3 m. The arrow points right. Complete: change in position = ___ m right.

lessons.takeaway: Say which number describes a location and which number describes a change. Check the small-step solutions only after you have marked the line.

lessons.title: One journey, two useful questions
lessons.kicker: 1 · See the whole path and the endpoints
lessons.intro: Start at 0 m, walk 6 m right, then walk 2 m left.
lessons.caption: The solid return leg is still part of the path. The dashed arrow joins only start and finish.

blocks.text: How much ground did you cover?
Your feet travelled both parts. Add their lengths.
What changed from start to finish?
You finish 4 m to the right of where you started. That change is displacement.
Distance has no direction. In a straight line, the sign of displacement gives its direction.

lessons.takeaway: Keep the two questions separate: “How much path?” → distance. “What change from the start?” → displacement.

lessons.title: Your starting position matters
lessons.kicker: 1 · Build the rule from a picture
lessons.intro: Start at +2 m, go to +7 m, then return to +4 m.
lessons.caption: The finish is +4 m, but the change from +2 m to +4 m is only +2 m.

blocks.text: A change is the new value minus the old value. Here, final position minus initial position gives:
A useful check: the size of the displacement cannot exceed the total path length.

lessons.takeaway: If you return to your start, the endpoint change is zero. Your walking is not erased: distance still counts every part. Try A1–A4 next.

lessons.title: A velocity–time graph tells a story
lessons.intro: Choose right as positive. Read the graph from left to right as time passes.
lessons.caption: The horizontal coordinate is time, not position. The line is not the shape of a road.

blocks.text: The line stays at +3 m/s. This means the object moves 3 m right in each second.
The line is at −1 m/s. The object now moves 1 m left in each second. Its speed is 1 m/s.
This interval lasts 6 − 4 = 2 s. Always subtract the two time readings.
The abrupt switch is an idealisation. It contributes no extra time or distance.

lessons.takeaway: A horizontal line above zero means steady motion. A line on v = 0 means rest. Below zero means motion in the chosen negative direction.

lessons.title: Why does graph area give a change in position?
lessons.kicker: 2 · Build the rectangle, then the rule
lessons.intro: At +3 m/s, each second adds another 3 m of rightward movement.
lessons.caption: Four one-second columns make 12 m. This is the +3 m/s part of the previous graph.

blocks.text: Adding the same change four times is multiplication.
On a v–t graph, height is velocity and width is duration. Their product is the rectangle area.
The seconds cancel, leaving metres. This rectangle rule requires constant velocity on the interval.

lessons.takeaway: Do not use the final velocity for an entire interval when velocity changes. In that case, use the actual area under the graph.

lessons.title: A return journey counts in two different ways
lessons.intro: Use the same graph: +3 m/s for 4 s, then −1 m/s for 2 s.
lessons.caption: Above zero adds rightward change. Below zero adds leftward change. Neither part is “negative walking”.

blocks.text: If you started at +5 m, you would finish at +15 m. The displacement would still be +10 m.

lessons.takeaway: A return can cancel an earlier change in position. It cannot cancel distance already travelled. Complete the two areas in A6 yourself.

lessons.title: Your turn · Complete the area reasoning
lessons.intro: The first region is worked for you. Complete the second region and combine them.
lessons.caption: First region: (+2 m/s) × (3 s) = +6 m of rightward change.

blocks.text: The interval starts at 3 s and ends at 5 s. Duration = 5 − 3 = ___ s.

The velocity is −1 m/s.
Second change = (−1) × ___ = ___ m.

lessons.takeaway: If a sign is confusing, point to the graph region and say whether the object moves right or left. Then check the small-step solutions.

lessons.title: When velocity rises steadily, use a triangle
lessons.intro: Velocity rises in a straight line from 0 to +4 m/s over 4 s.
lessons.caption: The sloping line cuts a 4 s by 4 m/s rectangle into two equal triangles.

blocks.text: That would describe +4 m/s for all four seconds. Here the object starts at rest and builds up speed.
The ½ comes from the triangle, not from a special motion formula.
All the graph lies at or above zero. So displacement is +8 m and distance is 8 m.
Use ½ × base × height only when the region between the graph and zero line is a triangle.

lessons.takeaway: Our triangle questions stay above zero. A straight segment away from zero may enclose a rectangle plus a triangle; do not call every sloping region a triangle.

core_calibrated.label: A1
core_calibrated.question: Start at +1 m. Walk 5 m left, then 3 m right. Find the final position, distance and displacement.
core_calibrated.recap: Start +1 m; 5 m left, then 3 m right.

solution.why: Position changes carry direction; path lengths do not.
solution.method: Start +1 m → turn −4 m → finish −1 m. Distance = 5 + 3 = 8 m. Displacement = −1 − (+1) = −2 m.
solution.answer: Final position −1 m; distance 8 m; displacement −2 m (left).
solution.keep: The final coordinate is not automatically the displacement.

core_calibrated.answer: Final position −1 m; distance 8 m; displacement −2 m (left).
hints: Keep the starting coordinate separate from the lengths walked.
Mark the start, the turning point and the finish on a number line.
The turning point is at +1 − 5 m. Find the finish next.
core_calibrated.workspace:
Start → turning point → finish
Final position: ____
Distance: ____   Displacement: ____

core_calibrated.label: A2
core_calibrated.question: An object moves from −2 m to +5 m without reversing. Find its distance and displacement. Explain the signs.
core_calibrated.recap: Move from −2 m to +5 m with no reversal.

solution.why: The route goes 2 m to zero and another 5 m right.
solution.method: From −2 m to zero is 2 m; then 5 m more to +5 m. Total change is 7 m right. This explains +5 − (−2) = +7 m.
solution.keep: Equal distance and displacement size require no reversal in this straight-line journey.

hints: Crossing the origin does not mean reversing direction.
Draw −2, 0 and +5 in order along the line.
The first part of the path, from −2 m to 0 m, is 2 m.
core_calibrated.workspace: Sketch the line and explain why crossing zero is not a turn.

core_calibrated.label: A3
core_calibrated.question: Two students start at 0 m and finish at +4 m. Must they have travelled the same distance? Draw two journeys to support your answer.
core_calibrated.recap: Same start 0 m and finish +4 m; compare possible distances.

solution.why: Endpoints fix displacement but leave the path undecided.
solution.method: One can go directly 0 → +4. Another can go 0 → +7 → +4. Their paths are 4 m and 7 + 3 m.
solution.answer: No. These distances are 4 m and 10 m; both displacements are +4 m.
solution.keep: A drawing can disprove an “always” claim.

core_calibrated.answer: No. These distances are 4 m and 10 m; both displacements are +4 m.
hints: The question fixes the endpoints, not the route.
Draw one direct route and one route with a turn.
For the turning route, choose a turning point beyond +4 m.
core_calibrated.workspace: Draw and label two routes. Keep the endpoints the same.

core_calibrated.label: A4
core_calibrated.question: A student walks 7 m right and then 3 m left. Find distance and displacement, taking right as positive.
core_calibrated.recap: Walk 7 m right, then 3 m left.

solution.why: Both legs count towards distance, while leftward motion reduces the rightward change.
solution.method: Both legs of the walk add to the total distance regardless of direction: 7 + 3. For displacement, keep the sign of each leg since right is positive; the rightward leg contributes +7 m and the leftward leg contributes −3 m, so add the signed changes.
solution.keep: Separate total path from net change.

hints: The student reverses direction after the first leg.
Use a path line and a separate start-to-finish arrow.
Add 7 m and 3 m to begin the distance calculation.
core_calibrated.workspace: Show the route or working that makes your answer clear.

core_calibrated.label: A5
core_calibrated.question: An object moves at +5 m/s for 3 s, then at −2 m/s for 2 s. Find displacement and distance for the whole journey.
core_calibrated.recap: Velocity +5 m/s for 3 s, then −2 m/s for 2 s.

solution.why: Each interval has constant velocity, so its signed area is velocity × duration.
solution.method: The changes are +5 × 3 = +15 m and −2 × 2 = −4 m. Add with signs for displacement; add sizes for distance.
solution.keep: Negative velocity gives negative displacement, not negative distance.

hints: One interval is rightward and one is leftward.
Draw two velocity–time rectangles on opposite sides of zero.
The first signed area is (+5 m/s) × (3 s).
core_calibrated.workspace: Show the route or working that makes your answer clear.

core_calibrated.label: A6
core_calibrated.question: Use the graph to find displacement and distance from 0 s to 5 s. Give a physical meaning for each area.
core_calibrated.recap: Graph: +4 m/s from 0–2 s, then −2 m/s from 2–5 s.

solution.why: Graph widths are durations. The second width is 5 − 2 = 3 s.
solution.method: Signed areas are +4 × 2 = +8 m and −2 × 3 = −6 m. For distance count both path lengths.
solution.answer: Displacement +2 m; distance 14 m. The parts mean 8 m right and 6 m left.
solution.keep: Read each width from its endpoints before multiplying.

core_calibrated.answer: Displacement +2 m; distance 14 m. The parts mean 8 m right and 6 m left.
hints: Read the duration of each horizontal segment.
Separate the two rectangular regions at t = 2 s.
For the first region, write (+4) × (2 − 0).
core_calibrated.workspace: Show the route or working that makes your answer clear.

core_calibrated.label: A7
core_calibrated.question: A constant velocity of +2.5 m/s is shown from 0 s to 8 s. Find displacement and distance. Why do their sizes agree?

solution.why: The graph is one positive rectangle; there is no reverse motion.
solution.method: Signed area = (+2.5 m/s) × (8 s) = +20 m. The same area size is the path length.
solution.answer: Displacement +20 m; distance 20 m. Their sizes agree because direction does not reverse.
solution.keep: A constant positive velocity produces steadily increasing position.

core_calibrated.answer: Displacement +20 m; distance 20 m. Their sizes agree because direction does not reverse.
hints: The velocity stays on one side of zero.
Draw the rectangle and label height and width with units.
Write area = (+2.5 m/s) × (8 s).
core_calibrated.workspace: Show the route or working that makes your answer clear.

core_calibrated.label: A8
core_calibrated.question: A trolley has the velocity–time graph shown. Find displacement and distance from 0 s to 6 s. Explain why 6 × 6 is unsuitable.
core_calibrated.recap: Velocity increases linearly from 0 to +6 m/s in 6 s.

solution.why: The graph forms a triangle. The trolley does not spend all 6 s at its final velocity.
solution.method: The triangle is half of a 6 s by 6 m/s rectangle: ½ × 6 × 6 = 18 m.
solution.answer: Displacement +18 m; distance 18 m. The graph never goes below zero.
solution.keep: Choose the shape from the actual graph, not just its final height.

core_calibrated.answer: Displacement +18 m; distance 18 m. The graph never goes below zero.
hints: The height grows during the interval.
Compare the region with the complete enclosing rectangle.
The rectangle would have area (6 s) × (6 m/s); use the fraction actually occupied.
core_calibrated.workspace: Show the route or working that makes your answer clear.

misconceptions.wrong_model: Distance and displacement are the same quantity.
misconceptions.observable_error: A learner reports total path length for a 'find the displacement' question, or vice versa.
misconceptions.diagnostic_question: A student walks 6 m right then 2 m left. Ask separately: how much ground did they cover, and how far are they from the start?
misconceptions.repair_explanation: Distance adds every path length walked, with no direction; displacement is only the change from initial to final position. They agree only when the motion never reverses direction.
misconceptions.micro_example: 0 m to 6 m to 4 m: distance is 6+2=8 m, but displacement is only 4-0=+4 m.
misconceptions.transfer_check: Give a return journey with a different turning point and ask for both quantities separately.

misconceptions.wrong_model: The height of a velocity-time graph directly gives distance travelled.
misconceptions.observable_error: A learner reads off the peak/final velocity value and reports it as the distance, instead of computing the area under the graph.
misconceptions.diagnostic_question: Show a v-t graph with a changing velocity and ask what the height of the line represents versus what the shaded region represents.
misconceptions.repair_explanation: Graph height is velocity, not distance. Distance/displacement is the area enclosed between the line and the time axis, split at every sign change for distance.
misconceptions.micro_example: A constant +3 m/s line for 4 s has height 3 m/s, but the enclosed area (and the actual displacement) is 12 m.
misconceptions.transfer_check: Give a triangular (accelerating) v-t graph and ask the learner to justify why the answer is not simply the final velocity.

guided_solutions.title: G1 · Positions and one-step changes
guided_solutions.text:
a. −2 m is 2 m left of the origin.
b. From +1 m, moving 3 m left ends at −2 m. The first arrow shows this move.
c. From −2 m to +3 m, move 2 m to zero, then 3 m right: displacement = +5 m (right). The second arrow shows this separate move.

guided_solutions.title: G2 · Duration, signed change and total path
guided_solutions.text:
a. Duration = 5 − 3 = 2 s.
b. Second change = (−1) × 2 = −2 m: 2 m left.
c. Displacement = +6 + (−2) = +4 m. Distance = 6 + 2 = 8 m.
The leftward part reduces the endpoint change, but still adds 2 m to the path.

left.text:
Distance: add every path length.
Displacement: the signed endpoint change.

Δx: displacement; xi: initial position;
xf: final position. Here, distance is 8 m and Δx is +4 m.

Check: distance ≥ |Δx|. Bars mean size.
Rebuild: trace the path, then compare its endpoints.

right.text:
Displacement: add signed areas.
Distance: add all the area sizes. Split at zero crossings.

Triangle size: ½ × base × height.
Graph above: Δx = +10 m; distance 14 m.
Check: (m/s) × s = m. Use a rectangle for constant velocity. Use ½ × base × height only for a triangular region; other straight segments may need rectangle + triangle.
